subject: religious-studies
title: Arguments for God: Cosmological, Teleological, Ontological
welcome_lead: Survey the three great families of theistic argument from antiquity to the twentieth century.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on Aquinas's Five Ways, Paley's design argument, and Anselm's ontological argument with major critics.
final_note: You have evaluated the cosmological, teleological, and ontological arguments and their classical critics.

concepts.def: Based on experience; cosmological and teleological arguments are a posteriori.
Independent of experience; the ontological argument is a priori.
Aquinas's five demonstrations of God's existence in Summa Theologiae I, Q.2, a.3.
Aquinas's Fifth Way: things without intelligence act for ends, so an intelligent director exists.
Paley's argument that the intricate purposiveness of organisms implies a designer.
Kant's Critique of Pure Reason objection to the ontological argument.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Five Ways of Summa Theologiae I, Q.2, a.3 are: (1) motion; (2) efficient causation; (3) contingency; (4) gradation of being; (5) governance of things lacking intelligence. The first three are cosmological, the fifth is teleological. The fourth, the henological argument, is often considered Platonic in inspiration.

William Paley's Natural Theology (1802) compares the watch to the natural world: its parts work together for a purpose. The intricate functionality of the eye, the wing, and the cardiovascular system implies an intelligent designer. Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) had pre-empted such arguments by questioning the analogy and the inference to one designer.

Anselm's Proslogion 2 (1078) argues that God, defined as that than which nothing greater can be conceived, must exist in reality as well as understanding. Gaunilo's perfect island objects; Anselm replies that only God's essence requires existence. Kant's Critique of Pure Reason (1781) argues existence is not a predicate but the positing of a subject. Plantinga's modal version (1974) revives the argument using possible-worlds semantics.
